# bombyx

> Drive isolated AI-agent VMs on a libvirt host, over SSH or
> on this machine. Rust CLI, derived from the rustbase
> template.

## Project Structure

Cargo workspace, CLI only:

- `crates/bombyx` — core library and CLI binary (paths below
  are `src/`-relative unless written in full)
  - `config.rs` — `Config` itself and `Config::load_project`,
    the one loader
  - `config/registry.rs` — the operator's own `config.toml`:
    the VM host, and a `[projects.<name>]` table per project
  - `config/host.rs` — where the VM host name comes from, the
    ranking between the registry's two `host` keys, the shape a
    host may take, and which directory the registry lives in
  - `config/transport.rs` — whether `host` names this very
    machine, and the `Transport` that answers
  - `name.rs` — validated `ScratchName` and `ProjectName`
    (one path segment each)
  - `remote.rs` — command construction for either route (pure)
  - `remote/command.rs` — `RemoteCommand` (`program`, `args`,
    `dir`, `stdin`) and how one renders for `--dry-run`, plus
    `Stdin`, which holds a payload and refuses to print it
  - `remote/write.rs` — `write_file`, which puts a generated
    file on the command's standard input rather than in an
    argument
  - `remote/probe.rs` — the read-only `doctor` probe scripts
  - `vagrantfile.rs` — renders the Vagrantfile, embeds the
    bootstrap script
  - `hostkeys.rs` — the two git hosts whose published ssh keys
    the guest fetches, and the URL and response shape of each
  - `plan.rs` — `Action` → ordered command list
  - `doctor.rs` — the check model; submodules own the rest
    - `doctor/probes.rs` — which probes run, reading a result
    - `doctor/readonly.rs` — proving a probe script writes nothing
    - `doctor/local.rs` — the workstation-side checks
    - `doctor/report.rs` — collecting and rendering findings
  - `listing.rs` — grouping projects by host, reading a
    `vagrant status` reply, rendering the `list` table
  - `term.rs` — text on its way to the terminal: line endings,
    host text made safe to print, clipping, the line of a
    failure that explains it
  - `tool.rs` — `PATH` lookup, never the working directory
  - `run.rs` — `Resolver` (looks every program up through
    `tool` before any command runs) with `execute` and `output`
    on it, plus the `Error` enum naming which stage failed.
    The only module that starts a `RemoteCommand`
  - `bin/bombyx/main.rs` — clap parsing, host-provenance
    reporting, driving `run`, the self-update ordering
  - `crates/bombyx/templates/bootstrap.sh` — the script the
    guest runs, identical for every project. The generated
    Vagrantfile marks the provisioner `privileged: false`, so
    the whole script runs as the box's SSH user, and no command
    in it raises privilege. The clone goes in `$HOME`, which
    that account owns, and a toolchain the project's script
    installs lands there too rather than in `/root`. A project
    needing root calls `sudo` from its own script
- `xtask` — build automation (not published)

No web crate, no frontend, no E2E suite, no deploy
subsystem — those were removed from the template.

## Model

bombyx never manages VMs directly. It generates a
Vagrantfile and a bootstrap script from the operator's own
`config.toml`, writes both onto the VM host and runs `vagrant`
there. Two routes carry that, and `config::transport` picks
between them by comparing `host` against this machine's own
name: `ssh <host> "<script>"` when they differ, `sh -c
"<script>"` when they match. The script is byte-identical
either way, because `sh -c` starts the same POSIX shell `ssh`
would have started on the host. `Config::transport()` reports
which route is in force. It is the one private field on
`Config`, which stops a caller choosing the route. `host` is
public and is a `HostName`, so an assignment to it carries a
checked value. bombyx derives the route once, while the config
loads, and never again, so an assignment to `host` can leave
`transport` naming the other route.

The VM host's own filesystem holds no project file; the guest
clones the repository itself once it is running. The
workstation reads nothing out of the project's directory
either, which is why `--project` names the project rather than
being worked out from where bombyx was run.

## Commands

```
bombyx up                 # write the generated files, boot the VM
bombyx provision          # re-run provisioning in the guest
bombyx down               # halt the VM
bombyx shell              # shell inside the VM (ssh -t)
bombyx status             # vagrant status
bombyx list               # every registered project and its VM state
bombyx doctor             # check preconditions, read-only
bombyx reset              # restore fresh-install snapshot
bombyx snapshot           # replace fresh-install snapshot
bombyx destroy <project>  # destroy the VM, remove its dir
bombyx scratch <name>     # boot a throwaway VM
bombyx discard <name>     # destroy a throwaway VM, remove its dir
bombyx self-update        # replace the binary; needs git, curl, tar
```

`up` ends by saving the `fresh-install` snapshot, and only
when the machine does not already hold it: the listing and the
save are one shell script with an `if` between them, so bombyx
reads no output and decides nothing. `snapshot` saves the same
name with `-f`, replacing whatever is there.

`destroy` requires the project name as confirmation.
`destroy` and `discard` both `rm -rf` the host directory after
destroying the VM; `remote_root` therefore rejects `..`.
`RemoteRoot`'s constructor is the only check on it, and serde
runs that constructor while the file parses.
`remote::remove_dir` carries a `debug_assert` that is a backstop
for a hand-built path, not the guard.

`list` reads the config file and asks every host named in it
what its projects are doing, one command per host rather than
one per project. The table goes to stdout; a host that does
not answer leaves its own projects `unknown`, puts one note on
stderr, and costs the other hosts nothing -- the `ssh` options
that bound a dead host are the ones `doctor` uses, from the
same builder. Any project left `unknown` makes the command
exit non-zero, which is wider than unreachability: a host that
answers without naming a state leaves the same gap.
`--offline` contacts no machine and drops the `STATE` column,
so only the config file itself can fail it. It is the only
subcommand that reads the config without naming one project.

Global flags: `--project <name>` (required by every subcommand
but `self-update` and `list`), `--config <path>` (the registry
file; defaults to `config.toml` in the config directory),
`--dry-run` (print the argv instead of running it).

## Configuration

One file, and it is the operator's own: `config.toml` in the
config directory, called **the registry** because it carries a
table per project. `--config <path>` reads a different file
instead. The operator commits that file nowhere, and bombyx
opens no file in the project's directory of its own accord --
`--config` and `BOMBYX_CONFIG_HOME` both point the loader
elsewhere, and `docs/trust-boundary.md` owns that
qualification.

`config.toml.sample` in the repository root is the only full
example, and a test loads it as shipped. The keys, in the order
a real file needs them, because a bare key binds to the table
header above it:

- `host` (file-wide) — the machine every project runs on unless
  its own table says otherwise
- `[projects.<name>]` — one per project. The table key is the
  project name, so no key inside repeats it. A name containing
  a `.` must be quoted, since TOML reads a bare dot as nesting
- `remote_root` (in a project's table) — optional, `~/vms`.
  Written below either table beneath it, this binds to that
  table instead and the whole file is refused
- `host` (in a project's table) — optional, for a project that
  runs on a machine of its own. It outranks the file-wide key
- `[projects.<name>.vm]` — required. `box`, `cpus` and `memory`
  have no defaults; `provider` is optional and defaults to
  `libvirt`. bombyx passes the provider to vagrant as
  `VAGRANT_DEFAULT_PROVIDER`, in front of every project vagrant
  call but the teardown, so a host that cannot supply it fails
  the boot. Vagrant ignores it once a machine exists, so
  changing the key needs a destroy first. `hyperv` parses and
  has never been run
- `[projects.<name>.source]` — required: `repo`, `ref`,
  `script`, what the guest clones and runs. `deploy_key` is
  optional: a path on the VM host naming the private key the
  guest clones a private repository with. `up`, `provision` and
  `scratch` check the file is on the VM host before creating
  anything (`remote::require_file`), the generated Vagrantfile
  uploads it to `/home/vagrant/.ssh/bombyx-deploy-key` before
  `bootstrap.sh` runs, and `bootstrap.sh` tightens it to 0600
  where the provisioner uploaded it -- owned by that user
  already -- names it on each `git` command it runs itself, and
  records the same command on the clone as `core.sshCommand` so
  the agent can push with it. The upload is conditional and
  carries no `raise` of its own, because `vagrant destroy` loads
  the Vagrantfile too. Whether a key was configured reaches the
  guest as `BOMBYX_DEPLOY_KEY`, always set, so the guest's own
  environment cannot answer it. Left out, no upload is rendered
  and no check is planned.
- Host-key verification, which is **independent of
  `deploy_key`** -- it applies to a public repository cloned
  over ssh just as much. A repository reached over ssh carries
  the git host's own identity into the guest.
  `RepoUrl::ssh_host` reads the host out of `repo` -- the one
  piece bombyx takes out of that value rather than passing whole
  -- and `hostkeys::for_host` looks it up in a table of two.
  `github.com` publishes its keys as JSON at
  `https://api.github.com/meta` and `bitbucket.org` publishes
  finished `known_hosts` lines at
  `https://bitbucket.org/site/ssh`. A hit sends three variables
  to the guest: `BOMBYX_GIT_HOST` (the table's lower-cased
  spelling, never the operator's), `BOMBYX_HOST_KEYS_URL` and
  `BOMBYX_HOST_KEYS_FORMAT` (`json` or `lines`). All three are
  empty for an `https` repository, which opens no ssh
  connection, and for a host the table does not hold.
  `bootstrap.sh` fetches the keys with `curl`, needs `jq` for
  the JSON shape, refuses when the response holds no line for
  that host, and then runs its own `clone` and `fetch` under
  `StrictHostKeyChecking=yes` with both known-hosts files named
  -- `UserKnownHostsFile` for what it fetched and
  `GlobalKnownHostsFile=/dev/null` for the system-wide pair;
  `docs/trust-boundary.md` says why naming the second is
  necessary rather than tidy. With all three empty it falls back
  to `StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new`, which trusts the host
  on first sight; `docs/trust-boundary.md` says what that costs.
  `ssh_host` also returns nothing for a port other than 22,
  because `known_hosts` spells such a host `[github.com]:2222`
  while the guest writes bare names. `GIT_SSH_COMMAND` is never
  exported: `bootstrap.sh` builds the options as `git_ssh` and
  names them on its own `clone` and `fetch`, one command at a
  time, because `exec` would otherwise hand them to the
  project's own script and pin every host it talks to. The clone
  keeps them as `core.sshCommand`, written when there is a
  deploy key or a fetched key file to carry
- `[projects.<name>.env]` — optional. Variables the project's
  own provisioning script reads, rendered into the generated
  Vagrantfile's provisioner beside bombyx's own set and sorted
  by name, so a re-run with an unchanged config writes a
  byte-identical file. Three rules on a name. It has to be
  spellable as a shell variable. It must not start with
  `BOMBYX_`, because a repeated key in a Ruby hash literal
  takes its last value and a project could otherwise choose
  which script bombyx runs. And it must not be one of the names
  in `NAMES_THAT_CHANGE_WHAT_BOOTSTRAP_DOES` in
  `crates/bombyx/src/config/env.rs` -- `PATH`, `SHELLOPTS`,
  `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT` and the rest -- because Vagrant puts the
  whole table in the provisioner's environment, which is
  `bootstrap.sh`'s own. `HOME` is on neither list and is the
  one to know about: bombyx clones into `$HOME/project`, so
  setting it moves the clone, and `bootstrap.sh` checks the
  value is absolute, present, writable, searchable and owned by
  that account before using it. A value carries the same
  `check_renderable` rule as `box`, `repo`, `ref`, `script` and
  `deploy_key`, so an empty one is refused and a variable is
  made absent by leaving the key out

The VM host belongs to the developer, not the project: each
person has their own hardware on their own network, so a
committed value would be wrong for everyone but its author --
and `destroy` runs `rm -rf` on whatever host is in force. Two
keys can name it, the project entry's own `host` and the
file-wide one, and the entry wins. See "Where bombyx looks for
the host" in `README.md` for the authoritative statement, and
`config::host::rank` for the code.

Every `host` in the registry is checked while the file is being
read, by `config::registry::parse` -- the file-wide key and
every project's, not only the one a command wants. Holding a
`Registry` is therefore the proof every host in it passed, so
`Registry::host` and `Registry::project_host` run no host rule
of their own. `config::host::rank`
does run it again, to build the winner into a `HostName`. Why
the rule runs in two places is argued once, in
`docs/architecture.md` under the heading "The host rule runs in
two places, and this is the owner".

The ranking itself is `config::host::rank`, which takes the
registry already read rather than opening it, because
`Config::load_project` needs the same copy of the file for the
project's other settings: a file edited between two reads could
supply a project host and a file-wide host that never
coexisted.

`Config::load_project(name, registry)` is the only loader.
`registry` is the file to read -- `--config` when the operator
passed one, `config::registry_file()` otherwise, and `None`
when the environment names no config directory at all. It reads
the `[projects.<name>]` table for every setting but the host,
ranks the host across the two keys, derives `Config::transport`
from the host that won, and returns a `(Config, HostOrigin)`
pair so the binary reports the winner rather than re-deriving
the rule. Its errors include
`RegistryNotFound` for a machine with no registry file,
`ProjectNotFound` for a file with no table for `name`, and
`HostMissing` when neither `host` key names one. An illegal
project name is refused before the file is looked for, so no
message ever advises a `[projects.<name>]` heading that the
parser would reject.

The binary is the only thing that reads `std::env`. A config
directory from the environment must be an anchored path -- a
relative one would resolve against the working directory and
take the host out of the repository.

bombyx opens no file in the project's directory at all. That is
a rule about files and not about everything a repository can
reach. A per-directory environment tool (`direnv`, `mise`, a CI
job) reads its settings from inside the clone, and a
`BOMBYX_CONFIG_HOME` set that way redirects bombyx to another
`config.toml` without printing a provenance line.

`remote_root` must be anchored (`/` or `~/`) and name at least
one directory below that anchor. bombyx creates, writes into and
-- on teardown -- deletes the directory it derives from the
value, so a root that resolves to a top-level directory is
refused when the config loads.

Ten config values are newtypes, and each constructor holds
every rule its field has: `RemoteRoot` in `config/root.rs`,
`HostName` in `config/host.rs`, `RepoUrl`, `ScriptPath` and
`GitRef` in `config/source.rs`, `DeployKeyPath` in
`config/deploy_key.rs`, `BoxName` in `config/vm.rs`, `EnvName`
and `EnvValue` in `config/env.rs`, and `ProjectName` in
`name.rs`. All of them but `HostName` carry
`#[serde(try_from = "String")]`, so serde refuses a bad value
while the file parses. `HostName` does not, because the message
for a bad host names the source key rather than the field and
serde cannot say which key it is reading; `config::host::checked`
attaches the `HostOrigin` instead. `RemoteRoot` also drops a
trailing slash, so the stored value is always in the form a path
join needs.

`Vm::cpus` and `Vm::memory` are `std::num::NonZeroU32`, which
is the whole rule either has. serde reads them through
`config::vm::positive_cpus` and `positive_memory`, declared with
`#[serde(deserialize_with = ...)]` rather than `try_from`. Both
delegate to `at_least_one`, which reads a plain `u32` and turns
every refusal into a `FieldError` naming the field. Why the
standard type alone would not name it is argued once, in
`docs/architecture.md` under the heading "What config values are
checked".

serde has therefore run every rule by the time a `Config`
exists, and no function checks a value afterwards. A `Vm`, a
`Source`, a `Project` or a `Config` that exists at all is one
whose values passed.

## Build Commands

```
cargo xtask validate          # the umbrella gate; see CLAUDE.md for the steps
cargo xtask check             # type-check all targets, run none
cargo xtask test [filter]     # tests only
cargo xtask clippy            # lint only
cargo xtask doc               # doc build + doc-link check
cargo xtask fmt               # format code
cargo xtask coverage          # coverage check (>=90% workspace, >=85% per module)
cargo xtask dupes             # duplication check (<=6%)
cargo xtask audit             # RUSTSEC advisories
```

`cargo xtask validate` is the canonical gate (`CLAUDE.md`
under Definition of Done lists the steps in run order);
`/release` runs it as the release gate; `/commit` does not run
it at all. A Claude Code Stop hook
(`.claude/hooks/stop-check.sh`) runs a faster subset -- fmt,
clippy, doc, test -- skipping coverage and duplication. Never use raw
`cargo test` / `cargo clippy`.

## Conventions

- Rust edition 2024, 80-column code and markdown
- `thiserror` in the library, `anyhow` in the binary
- `#[forbid(unsafe_code)]`, clippy pedantic, zero warnings
- Logic lives in the library: `src/bin/` is excluded from
  coverage, so code there ships untested
- `remote.rs` builds commands but never spawns processes,
  which is what keeps it testable without a VM host; `run.rs`
  is the one module that starts one
- a generated file travels on the command's standard input, not
  in an argument, because every logged-in account on a machine
  can list what other accounts are running, arguments included --
  that is what `ps` prints. `Stdin` has no
  `Display` and a `Debug` reporting only a length, so a payload
  cannot reach the terminal by accident
- the registry is the operator's own file rather than a
  committed one, and every field is still validated against an
  allowlist. `host` reaching `ssh` as `-oProxyCommand=...`
  would be local RCE, and the rule holds on both routes because
  the same file carried to another machine takes the `ssh` one
- Remote paths go through `quote_remote_path`, which leaves
  a leading `~` outside the quotes — a POSIX shell does not
  expand `~` inside single quotes

## Claude Code Skills

| Skill | Purpose |
|-------|---------|
| `/check` | Type-check all targets, running none |
| `/test` | Run tests with agent-friendly output |
| `/validate` | Full quality pipeline |
| `/commit` | Commit with diary and CHANGELOG (no reviewing) |
| `/review` | Review the work with the three reviewers, one at a time; commits nothing |
| `/release` | Cut a SemVer release |
| `/retrospect` | Workflow retrospective |
| `/todo` | Capture a work item into `docs/todo.md` |
| `/implement` | Plan + execute a captured item |
| `/issue` | Work a GitHub issue end to end |
| `/architect` | Architecture guide |
| `/short` | Restate the reply above in under 40 words |
| `/template-sync` | Pull upstream rustbase improvements |
| `/template-improve` | Log feedback about the template |
